original_value: AbstractSYBA (SYnthetic Bayesian Accessibility) is a fragment-based method for the rapid classification of organic compounds as easy- (ES) or hard-to-synthesize (HS). It is based on a Bernoulli naïve Bayes classifier that is used to assign SYBA score contributions to individual fragments based on their frequencies in the database of ES and HS molecules. SYBA was trained on ES molecules available in the ZINC15 database and on HS molecules generated by the Nonpher methodology. SYBA was compared with a random forest, that was utilized as a baseline method, as well as with other two methods for synthetic accessibility assessment: SAScore and SCScore. When used with their suggested thresholds, SYBA improves over random forest classification, albeit marginally, and outperforms SAScore and SCScore. However, upon the optimization of SAScore threshold (that changes from 6.0 to – 4.5), SAScore yields similar results as SYBA. Because SYBA is based merely on fragment contributions, it can be used for the analysis of the contribution of individual molecular parts to compound synthetic accessibility. SYBA is publicly available athttps://github.com/lich-uct/sybaunder the GNU General Public License.

result.paraphrase: AbstractSYBA (SYnthetic Bayesian Accessibility) is a fragment-based approach for quickly classifying organic compounds as easy to synthesize (ES) or hard to synthesize (HS). It uses a Bernoulli naïve Bayes classifier to assign SYBA score contributions to individual fragments according to their frequencies in a database of ES and HS molecules. SYBA was trained on ES molecules from the ZINC15 database and on HS molecules produced by the Nonpher methodology. It was benchmarked against a random forest used as a baseline, as well as two other synthetic accessibility assessment methods: SAScore and SCScore. With their recommended thresholds, SYBA slightly improves on random forest classification and outperforms SAScore and SCScore. However, after optimizing the SAScore threshold from 6.0 to – 4.5, SAScore gives results similar to SYBA. Since SYBA relies solely on fragment contributions, it can be used to analyze the contribution of individual molecular parts to a compound’s synthetic accessibility. SYBA is publicly available at https://github.com/lich-uct/syba under the GNU General Public License.
